generatedProse.concept-context: Every subject articulates criticality in a language of its own. Connectives such as 'however' and 'therefore' signal how claims relate, while hedges such as 'arguably' or 'provisional' mark how far a finding can be pressed. A field's own precise terms carry judgements in a single word, so choosing them exactly is itself a critical act.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing up the same judgement about a disputed finding.

{{learner-a}} writes: this source is good, and the other is not as good, so the first is better. The judgement is there in outline, but the language is flat. Nothing signals how the claims relate, and no term carries the meaning a reader in the field would expect. The reasoning move cannot be seen.

{{learner-b}} writes: the first source is the more robust; however, its result rests on a single, untested case, so its advantage is provisional rather than settled. The connectives mark the critical moves, and a precise term such as untested carries a judgement of its own. The same position is now articulated with precision.

Both students reached a similar view. Only {{learner-b}} articulated it in the language of criticality.
generatedProse.summary: In any subject, articulating criticality means using connectives, hedges and precise terms deliberately, so the reasoning is visible in the writing. You can now signal critical moves, explain why a field's own terms carry critical meaning, and choose wording that articulates a judgement exactly. With synthesis, judgement and language in place, you can be critical on the page.

check.body: In the worked example, why did {{learner-b}}'s precise term do more critical work than {{learner-a}}'s everyday word?

items.text: It carried a defined meaning in the field, so it made a judgement the vague word left unsaid.
It made the writing sound more formal.
It was longer and more technical.
It avoided repeating an earlier word.

feedback.correct: That's right. A defined field term states a judgement the everyday word leaves unsaid.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the meaning the field attaches to the term.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The term did critical work because it carried a defined meaning in the field, stating a judgement the vague word left unsaid. Formality, length or variety are not the point.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
